doc.title: Laurena Diggs and Carrie Boote Interview, 1959-05-25

chapter: Punch Miller and musicians she knew
title: Peck Gauman, Fred Reed and pianists on Chicago's north side
summary: She describes Gauman passing for white, solo pianists in white cabarets, Fred Reed's earnings, and Punch Miller's singing fame.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: No. Well, you know, most, if they were connected with any, any of the bands around there, mostly I would know them. But a lot of those, uh, piano players, now, they had a fellow here named Peg Gauman. Gauman. Gauman. He was a colored fellow, but he always passed, and he played down in the district here. Now, he left here, and he went to Chicago. But he, he passed for White, and he played with the orchestra at the Chicago Theater for years. And, of course, he was a very good piano player. But by him going there, and getting out of circulation, and went on the north side, well, we, we never knew anything about him. But he was a boyfriend of my cousin's, and actually I knew him for years from being associated with her. But he played now at the Chicago Theater for years. Peck Gauman. He used to play in the, on Bourbon Street, Peck, played piano. Very handsome fellow. And, uh, and you see, when you go there, and if you get on the north side, in any of those places, just with a small band, uh, uh, and, and a lot of those colored fellows, when they go there, they, like their solo band, like their solo piano player, they play and sing between times, just like when the big band start playing, then you, they have a small little piano, and then you, it's like a little, uh, on a flat phone. You know, just a tiny piano. But after the dance is over, you get, um, this little piano, and you can push it from one table to the other, around the, uh, the dance floor, and if you have a party here, and anything you want to hear, well, I sing it for you, and then the other, and they go around. But once, when you get over there, you're just out of circulation with the public. You know, you're all right over on the north side, but just like most of the colored people on the south side, they wouldn't know what's happening, you know, in these other places. Because, now, you're welcome to go if you want to, but they have all the fun they want in their own neighborhood, and they'd very seldom go over there. Well, now, so many of the boys have went over there, and they got popular financially, but they are not known because they do this solo way by themselves. Now, they have a boy, he isn't, uh, uh, from here, he, he worked with Punch, Fred Reed. Now, he, uh, plays piano, and before they were making this big money, he was making around $500 a week. But he was a very fine piano player. He's from Jackson, Mississippi, but he played with all the Louisiana boys, and everybody thought he was from New Orleans. Now, he plays by himself. You know, after the orchestra plays, he and the teams. And the women just come from all over just to hear him sing and play. Fred Reed is his name. And, uh, but nobody knows him on the south side as a great pianist, because he's over there in this white cabaret, and he's making his money. And, uh, the being popular among the other people don't mean nothing. Financials, you know, is what he was interested in. But he played with Punch and, uh, Francois for a while, and then when he went there, well, people have forgotten about Fred no more, and they know about the buildings. He's buying a car or something like that, but his sister and I are very good friends, and she said that his salary is $500 a week. And, uh, I don't know if that has anything to do with tips or anything, because when some of them, they call you to play, they may hand you $5 or $10. Some of this weak women, they hand you $5 now. Now, you take Punch. He used to, uh, sing, You Got Me Between the Devil and the Deep Blue Sea, and he used to sing Marie. And my phone would ring off the walls when he would broadcast, you know, on the radio, sing, and he was very popular at that time, you know. And, uh, just, him singing made him so popular, but that's the way it was with Fred. When he got over there, the women seemed to like his playing and his voice, and he just buried himself there, and he's doing very well financially.
